Hurtful
hurt'ful
a. (causing injury or loss; of a rebellious city, a sword, and the lusts that drown men)
From hurt — Old French hurter, to strike or collide — with -ful. The Greek at 1 Timothy 6:9 is blaberos, injurious, from blapto, to harm; the word occurs only there in the New Testament.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Paul supplies the decisive occurrence: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition” (1 Timothy 6:9). Three things are worth noting. The subject is not the rich but they that will be rich — the desire, not the estate. The lusts are called both foolish and hurtful, so that folly and injury are joined. And the verb drown is the word for a ship sinking with all hands; these desires do not merely disappoint, they submerge. The next verse gives the root: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:10) — note again that it is the love, not the money, and the wounds are self-inflicted. The Psalmist uses the word of a weapon: the LORD “delivereth David his servant from the hurtful sword” (Psalm 144:10). And Solomon observed the strangest case of all: “riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt” (Ecclesiastes 5:13) — a hoard that injures the man who keeps it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hurtful as injurious, mischievous, causing loss or damage, and notes it is applied to what injures either estate or character.

expand to see more

HURTFUL, a. Injurious; mischievous; occasioning loss or destruction; tending to impair or destroy.

Negligence is hurtful to property; intemperance is hurtful to health.

HURT, n. A wound; a bruise; whatever gives pain to the body.

2. Damage; injury; loss.

3. Mischief; harm as to the mind or character.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 6:9 — "But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition."

1 Timothy 6:10 — "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows."

Psalm 144:10 — "It is he that giveth salvation unto kings: who delivereth David his servant from the hurtful sword."

Ecclesiastes 5:13 — "There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt."

Modern Corruption

Harm has replaced sin as the primary moral category, so that conduct is judged by reported injury rather than by God's law.

expand to see more

The dominant moral framework of the age reduces ethics to a single question: does this cause harm? On that account whatever injures no one who complains is permitted, and whatever someone reports as injurious is condemned regardless of what God has said. The framework is attractive because it appears humane and requires no revelation; it fails because it has no fixed measure of injury and no account of offences against God. Scripture uses hurtful freely — Paul calls the lusts of the would-be rich hurtful — but always inside a prior category. The lusts are sinful first; that they drown men is the consequence, not the definition. # voice-lock-ok: harmful: names the harm-only framework in order to rebut it

The practical difference shows in 1 Timothy 6. A purely harm-based ethic cannot condemn the desire to be rich, since the desire injures no one and the man himself consents to it. Paul condemns it, and then describes the harm that follows: a snare, a drowning, a piercing through with many sorrows. The order matters. Recovering it restores both halves of moral reasoning — that sin is defined by God's law rather than by the tally of complaints, and that God's law is not arbitrary, since what He forbids does in fact ruin those who pursue it. Ecclesiastes 5:13 is the same lesson in miniature: a man's hoard, kept safely, to his hurt.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek blaberos, injurious — 1 Timothy 6:9; buthizo, to sink or drown — the same verse; Hebrew ra, evil or harmful — Psalm 144:10, Ecclesiastes 5:13.

expand to see more

Greek blaberos — injurious, hurtful; 1 Timothy 6:9, its only New Testament occurrence.

Greek buthizo — to plunge into the deep, to sink a ship; the verb rendered drown in the same verse.

Greek peripeiro — to pierce through; 1 Timothy 6:10, of self-inflicted sorrows.

Hebrew ra — evil, bad, harmful; Psalm 144:10 of the sword, Ecclesiastes 5:13 of the hoard.

Old French hurter, to strike or collide — the source of English hurt.

Usage

"“They that will be rich” — the desire is the danger, not the estate."

"“Which drown men in destruction” — the verb for a ship going down with all hands."

"“Riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt” — the hoard that injures its keeper."
